\title{\textbf{Autonomous Enterprise Data Analysis via Semantic Schema Grounding, Plan Validation, and Multi-Turn SQL AST Repair}}
\author{
  \textbf{Mevin Jose} \\

\begin{abstract}
While Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong conversational capabilities, enterprise natural language interfaces to relational databases (Text-to-SQL) routinely fail due to schema hallucinations, invalid join topologies, aggregation grain mismatch, and SQL dialect incompatibilities. In this paper, we present an autonomous multi-stage data analyst agent architecture that integrates: (1) Graph-Guided Semantic Schema RAG for precision table and column subgraph extraction; (2) Structured DAG Query Planning with deterministic pre-execution constraint validation; and (3) AST-Level SQL Semantic Verification with closed-loop multi-turn self-correction and grain repair. We evaluate our system on an audited 500-query enterprise benchmark spanning 8 distinct business domains over a 100,000-order relational data warehouse (the Olist Brazilian E-Commerce dataset). Our Phase~10 system achieves an empirical \textbf{\HeadlineEquivalentAccuracy{} Equivalent Match Accuracy} (\HeadlineEquivalentCILower{}--\HeadlineEquivalentCIUpper{}, 95\% Wilson Score CI), \textbf{\HeadlineExactMatchAccuracy{} Exact Match Accuracy}, and \textbf{\HeadlineSQLExecutionSuccess{} SQL Execution Success} with zero provider timeouts or rate-limit failures. In a controlled component ablation, AST semantic verification delivers substantial execution and semantic stability improvements over unverified planners. An exhaustive audit of the \TotalRepairTriggered{} repair events demonstrates that agent self-repair is a nuanced, dual-edged mechanism: while repair maintained \RepairSyntaxSuccessRate{} syntactic execution validity, preserved \RepairMaintainedCount{} already-correct queries, and truly recovered \RepairTrulyRecoveredCount{} broken queries, over-aggressive repair rules caused \RepairHarmedFalsePositiveCount{} false-positive regressions. Furthermore, we report an AST failure taxonomy classifying \TotalFailuresAnalyzed{} non-equivalent queries, a controlled 50-query synthetic perturbation robustness study across 5 vectors, and latency-cost configuration trade-off trajectories. We conclude with a candid discussion of limitations, including single-schema specificity, inference latency overhead, and typographical vulnerability.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Natural language interfaces to relational databases (Text-to-SQL) promise to democratize data analytics for non-technical stakeholders \cite{yu2018spider,li2023bird}. However, real-world multi-table relational warehouses (e.g., enterprise ERPs, e-commerce data platforms) present severe challenges for monolithic zero-shot LLM prompting:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Schema Grounding Hallucinations:} LLMs frequently invent nonexistent columns (e.g., querying \texttt{order\_amount} instead of \texttt{price}), assume undocumented relational keys, or join tables across disconnected foreign-key topologies.
    \item \textbf{Aggregation Grain Inconsistencies:} Complex business metrics require computing aggregations across distinct dimensional grains (e.g., computing order item revenue before joining customer demographics to avoid join fan-out multiplication). Unconstrained LLMs frequently produce syntactically valid queries that yield erroneous numerical figures.
    \item \textbf{Dialect Traps \& Engine Incompatibilities:} Database engines exhibit syntax discrepancies (such as SQLite's \texttt{strftime('\%Y-\%m', ts)} vs. PostgreSQL's \texttt{DATE\_TRUNC('month', ts)}), triggering execution runtime exceptions.
    \item \textbf{Agent Hallucinatory Drift:} Iterative agentic loops without deterministic AST guards often oscillate between syntax errors without converging on the correct semantic answer.
\end{enumerate}

To address these foundational failure modes, we propose an autonomous, multi-stage architecture with deterministic validation gates at every stage. Rather than relying on unconstrained end-to-end generation, our system decouples retrieval, logical query planning, deterministic plan validation, AST semantic verification, and closed-loop repair.

\section{Related Work}
\paragraph{Text-to-SQL Benchmarks and Methods.}
Large-scale benchmarks such as Spider \cite{yu2018spider} and BIRD \cite{li2023bird} have driven Text-to-SQL research toward complex multi-table joins, nested subqueries, and large database execution. Decomposition-based approaches like DIN-SQL \cite{pourreza2023dinsql} and MAC-SQL \cite{wang2024macsql} demonstrate that breaking down Text-to-SQL into sub-problems (schema linking, classification, SQL generation, self-correction) outperforms monolithic prompting. Our work builds upon this insight by introducing a deterministic, AST-level validation and repair layer that inspects query structure independently of model self-consistency.

\paragraph{Schema Linking and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).}
Retrieval-Augmented Generation \cite{lewis2020rag,asai2023selfrag} has become the standard technique for grounding LLMs in external knowledge. In database querying, schema linking requires retrieving relevant tables, columns, and foreign-key join paths. Prior work has used dense retrieval or BM25 keyword matching; we augment hybrid dense-sparse retrieval with explicit foreign-key graph traversal to preserve schema connectivity.

\paragraph{Agentic Architectures and Self-Correction.}
Agentic frameworks such as ReAct \cite{yao2022react} and Reflexion \cite{shinn2023reflexion} leverage iterative reasoning, acting, and verbal reinforcement. In Text-to-SQL, execution-guided self-correction feeds database compiler errors back to the LLM \cite{gao2023text2sql}. However, as our empirical audit reveals, relying solely on execution feedback is dangerous: 96\% of post-repair queries execute cleanly, yet over 21\% suffer from semantic false-positive regressions.

\section{System Architecture}
Our architecture decomposes Text-to-SQL synthesis into an observable, 5-stage pipeline (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}):

\subsection{Graph-Guided Semantic Schema RAG}
Instead of overloading LLM context windows with entire database schemas, our retriever combines BM25 keyword matching, dense embedding retrieval (SentenceTransformers), and foreign-key graph traversal. Given a question, the retriever extracts the minimal required schema subgraph, achieving \HeadlineTablePrecision{} precision and \HeadlineTableRecall{} recall across the 500-query benchmark.

\subsection{Analytics Query Planner \& Plan Validator}
Before emitting SQL syntax, the planner synthesizes a structural JSON DAG declaring target metrics, grain dimensions, required tables, and explicit join paths. The deterministic \texttt{PlanValidator} statically inspects this DAG against the live database catalog, pruning hallucinated columns or invalid foreign-key joins prior to code generation.

\subsection{SQL Semantic Verifier \& AST-Guided Closed-Loop Repair}
Generated SQL queries are parsed into Abstract Syntax Trees (AST) via SQLGlot \cite{sqlglot2023}. The \texttt{SQLSemanticVerifier} inspects:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Dialect Compliance:} Converts dialect-specific functions (\texttt{DATEDIFF}, \texttt{DATE\_TRUNC}) to canonical SQLite idioms (\texttt{strftime}, \texttt{julianday}).
    \item \textbf{Join Fan-Out \& Grain Consistency:} Detects missing \texttt{GROUP BY} keys and unjoined cartesian products.
    \item \textbf{Canonical Metric Source Mapping:} Enforces standardized column sources (e.g., \texttt{order\_items.price} for revenue).
\end{itemize}

When violations occur, the verifier triggers targeted closed-loop repair prompts detailing the specific AST constraint violation.

\section{Experimental Methodology}

\subsection{Data Warehouse \& Benchmark Design}
We evaluate our system on the Brazilian E-Commerce relational data warehouse (Olist dataset \cite{olist2018kaggle}):
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{9 Relational Tables:} \texttt{customers}, \texttt{orders}, \texttt{order\_items}, \texttt{order\_payments}, \texttt{order\_reviews}, \texttt{products}, \texttt{sellers}, \texttt{geolocation}, and \texttt{product\_category\_name\_translation}.
    \item \textbf{Scale:} 100,000+ orders, 112,650 order items, and 1,000,000+ geolocation records.
    \item \textbf{Benchmark Corpus:} A frozen 500-query benchmark dataset (\texttt{benchmark\_dataset\_500.json}) stratified across 8 commercial domains and 3 difficulty tiers.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Evaluation Metrics \& Semantic Definitions}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Equivalent Match Rate (95\% Wilson CI):} Evaluates whether executed SQL results match ground-truth values under row-order invariance (comparing row multisets via Counters) with numerical tolerance ($\epsilon=0.01$) and string normalization. Positional column semantics are preserved.
    \item \textbf{Exact Match Rate:} Strict character-for-character row and column name equality.
    \item \textbf{SQL Execution Success Rate:} Percentage of queries executing without runtime database exceptions.
    \item \textbf{Table Precision \& Recall:} Semantic alignment of queried tables vs. ground-truth tables.
\end{itemize}

\section{Controlled Component Ablation Study}
To measure the marginal contribution of each architectural stage, we evaluated four controlled configurations across 100 benchmark queries:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Config A (RAG Only):} Direct single-table fallback heuristic; semantic verifier explicitly OFF.
    \item \textbf{Config B (RAG + Planner):} LLM query planner with plan validation; semantic verifier explicitly OFF.
    \item \textbf{Config C (RAG + Planner + Verifier):} LLM query planner with AST semantic verifier explicitly ON.
    \item \textbf{Config D (Full System):} Full multi-stage pipeline with evaluator agent; semantic verifier explicitly ON.
\end{itemize}

\IfFileExists{tables/tab_phase_progression.tex}{\input{tables/tab_phase_progression.tex}}{\input{../tables/tab_phase_progression.tex}}

The ablation confirms that activating the AST Semantic Verifier (Config~C vs. Config~B) rescues planner queries, substantially increasing SQL execution reliability (34.0\% $\rightarrow$ 65.0\%) and equivalent accuracy (15.0\% $\rightarrow$ 26.0\%).

\subsection{Critical Empirical Takeaways on Self-Repair Dynamics}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Execution Success $\neq$ Semantic Repair:} While \RepairSyntaxSuccessRate{} of post-repair queries executed without SQLite syntax errors, only 52.5\% produced semantically correct results. Describing execution success as repair recovery is methodologically invalid.
    \item \textbf{The False-Positive Regression Hazard:} Across the \TotalRepairTriggered{} triggered cases, 71 were already semantically correct before repair was considered; among these, \RepairHarmedFalsePositiveCount{} were degraded by repair (e.g., when the repair agent modified valid date filters or altered join keys). This highlights an essential trade-off: rule-based verifiers risk inducing regressions when applied indiscriminately.
\end{enumerate}

\section{AST Failure Taxonomy Analysis}
We analyzed all \TotalFailuresAnalyzed{} non-equivalent queries using AST diffing against ground truth SQL (Figure~\ref{fig:taxonomy}):
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Schema Missing Join Path (37 queries, 26.8\%):} Omission of intermediate bridging tables (e.g., joining \texttt{order\_reviews} to \texttt{customers} without \texttt{orders}).
    \item \textbf{Semantic Aggregation Mismatch (32 queries, 23.2\%):} Discrepancies in aggregation function types (\texttt{AVG} vs \texttt{SUM}).
    \item \textbf{Semantic Filter Omission (31 queries, 22.5\%):} Missing domain predicates such as \texttt{order\_status = 'delivered'}.
    \item \textbf{Schema Hallucinated Table (17 queries, 12.3\%):} Synthesizing nonexistent subqueries or table aliases.
    \item \textbf{Grain / GROUP BY Mismatch (14 queries, 10.1\%):} Grouping by year-month string aliases rather than raw date expressions.
    \item \textbf{Semantic Ranking Order Mismatch (7 queries, 5.1\%):} Inverted or missing \texttt{ORDER BY} clauses.
\end{enumerate}

To examine pipeline sensitivity to controlled lexical and semantic shifts, we evaluated a deterministic 50-query synthetic perturbation suite ($N=50$, 10 queries per vector across 8 domains; Table~\ref{tab:robustness} and Figure~\ref{fig:robustness}). We emphasize that this suite tests specific local perturbation robustness rather than broad out-of-distribution cross-domain generalization.

\section{Limitations \& Threats to Validity}
We explicitly document the scientific and operational limitations of this study:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Single Data Warehouse Schema:} All experiments are conducted on the Brazilian E-Commerce (Olist) data warehouse (9 tables, 100k orders). While representative of enterprise star/snowflake schemas, this study does not establish zero-shot transfer to medical, financial, or graph databases without domain-specific schema RAG tuning.
    \item \textbf{Inference Latency Overhead:} Multi-stage planning, validation, and repair incur a mean latency of \HeadlineMeanLatency{} ($p95$: \HeadlinePNinetyFiveLatency{}) and higher token usage compared to single-shot prompting.
    \item \textbf{Hard Query Complexity Ceiling:} Equivalent match accuracy drops to 44.55\% on hard-tier queries and 23.26\% on complex aggregated multi-column tables, reflecting challenges in multi-step CTE nesting.
    \item \textbf{Typographical Vulnerability:} Under character-level typo perturbations, accuracy drops by 30.0\% (57.1\% retention rate), indicating the need for fuzzy, typo-tolerant schema indexing.
    \item \textbf{False-Positive Repair Regressions:} 21.8\% of repair attempts degraded previously correct queries, underscoring the need for uncertainty-gated verification.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}
We presented an autonomous multi-stage data analyst agent architecture combining semantic schema RAG, structured plan validation, and AST SQL verification. Evaluated on an audited 500-query benchmark over a 100,000-order enterprise warehouse, the system achieved \textbf{\HeadlineEquivalentAccuracy{}} Equivalent Match Accuracy and \textbf{\HeadlineSQLExecutionSuccess{}} SQL Execution Success. Our component ablation and granular 101-case repair audit provide foundational empirical evidence on the necessity and trade-offs of deterministic semantic verification in enterprise Text-to-SQL systems.
